title: Who Is Teaching Young Men to Live?
author: Thinking West
summary: This essay diagnoses the crisis of young male formation by contrasting the intentional mentorship structures of historical societies with the therapy-app culture of the present. The author argues that prior generations understood maturity as cultivated through intentional initiation—apprenticeship, religious formation, the Grand Tour—while modern culture assumes maturity will happen on its own through access to information, prescribing therapeutic fixes to symptoms rather than addressing the absence of formative structures. Using Dante's Virgil as a model of the wise mentor, the essay argues that guidance is not a supplement to living well but constitutive of it: Dante does not find his way through introspection but through a guide who teaches him to see reality correctly. The piece contends that therapy is a rescue operation for when formation has failed, and that a culture with genuine mentorship for young men would need far less of it. The author calls for fathers and men in communities to take responsibility for forming boys rather than outsourcing it to institutions or online influencers, warning that boys who lack impressive men to emulate will find them elsewhere.
points: Historical societies from ancient initiation rites through religious schools to the Grand Tour all shared a common assumption: maturity is cultivated through intentional formation by exemplary guides, not achieved through information access alone.
Therapy is a rescue operation for when formation has failed; a culture with genuine mentorship would need far less of it, because Virgil-style guidance addresses the root rather than the symptom.

Dante's Virgil is not merely a navigator but a moral instructor who teaches Dante to see reality correctly—the kind of role that poets held in antiquity because beautiful language conveys truths about the world and interior life.

Young men today are drawn to online influencers who project strength, competence, and aspiration because those influencers are filling the role that impressive men in community once played; blaming the 'manosphere' without asking why churches and institutions failed to offer a more compelling model misidentifies the problem.

The older understanding of guidance precludes the need for therapy: 'Mentorship and formation are the way we, throughout our lives, gain the wisdom and virtues necessary to avoid falling into mental roadblocks, sins, and personal problems that require therapy.'
quotes: For anyone paying attention, it's clear that young people, especially young men, are struggling. Many today are anxious and lonely, searching for meaning, direction, purpose… anything. Whether they know it or not, they're looking for someone who can help them figure out life.

Previous generations suffered wars, economic collapse, disease, and personal tragedy on a scale that most will never experience. Yet they didn't have on-demand therapy to talk through their problems. Instead, they relied on something else.

All these educational experiences promoted a common vision of the actualized human person. Western societies, particularly those shaped by Christianity, had a more coherent answer on what maturity meant. A good man was not simply someone who achieved personal satisfaction, but rather someone who practiced virtue, fulfilled obligations, served others, and oriented their life toward the highest good.

Therapy is the rescue operation when things have gone awry. Mentorship and formation are the way we, throughout our lives, gain the wisdom and virtues necessary to avoid falling into mental roadblocks, sins, and personal problems that require therapy.

Like Dante waking dazed in a wood, they are lacking direction. They have ambition and potential, but little vision of what to use those gifts for. Dante doesn't discover the way himself; nor does he soon discover the right way through introspection, or as we might say today by 'finding himself'. No, he must be led by a guide.

Boys are turning to online influencers because many of those men project strength, competence, seriousness, and aspiration. Do not blame the 'manosphere' without asking why church leaders have failed to offer a more compelling model of manhood.
